title: Ensure sustainable wild flower harvesting operations

lessons.title: Planning a sustainable harvesting operation
lessons.html:
The manager's responsibility

At NQF level 4 you are responsible for the whole harvesting operation: permits, harvest planning, teams, quality and conservation outcomes. The goal is a reliable supply of quality wild-harvested fynbos and other wild flowers while keeping populations and habitats healthy for the long term.

Legal compliance

  • Obtain and keep current the permits required by the provincial nature conservation authority for harvesting, transporting and selling wild flora, especially protected species. Know the conditions attached.
  • Ensure written landowner permission for every harvesting site.
  • Comply with labour laws (BCEA, OHS Act 85 of 1993) for harvesting teams.
  • Comply with export phytosanitary requirements for export product.

Resource inventory

Map harvesting blocks and record for each: species present, estimated population, plant age and condition, fire history, alien plant infestation and sensitive areas such as wetlands and threatened species. Get specialist input where needed.

The harvest plan

  • Harvest limits: the proportion of flowering stems per plant and per population that may be cut, as set by the applicable code of practice, permit conditions or ecological advice.
  • Rotation and rest: blocks are rested between harvests to recover, and recently burnt or young veld is not harvested until plants have matured and set seed as advised.
  • Species-specific rules: some species are reseeders (killed by fire, rely on seed) and need higher seed retention; resprouters recover from rootstocks. Harvest rules should reflect this.
  • Exclusion zones: riparian areas, wetlands and populations of threatened species.
  • Fire management: firebreaks and coordination with the local fire protection association.
  • Alien clearing programme integrated with harvesting.

Market alignment

Match the harvest plan to orders and specifications so stems are not cut and wasted. Over-cutting for uncertain orders damages both resources and margins.

lessons.title: Controlling operations, monitoring and certification
lessons.html:
Team management

  • Train harvesters in species identification, harvest limits, cutting technique, quality specs, safety and veld etiquette.
  • Appoint team leaders responsible for compliance in the field.
  • Provide PPE (gloves, hats, long sleeves, boots, sunscreen), water, first aid kits and transport.
  • Use payment systems that reward quality and compliance, not just volume, so pickers are not pushed to over-harvest.

Field controls

  • Issue daily harvest instructions: block, species, quantities and specs.
  • Spot-check plants after harvesting to confirm limits were followed.
  • Record stems harvested per block, species and team.
  • Control access to blocks to stop illegal picking and report poaching.

Post-harvest quality

Move stems to shade quickly, hydrate or treat according to product protocols, grade and bunch to specification, and maintain the cold chain where needed. Record rejects and their causes.

Ecological monitoring

  • Fixed-point photographs and simple plot counts of plants, flowering and seedlings in harvested and unharvested blocks.
  • Records of post-fire recruitment of seedlings.
  • Alien plant density mapping.
  • Observations of pollinators such as sugarbirds and sunbirds.

Compare trends year on year. If populations decline, reduce harvest limits or extend rest periods.

Certification and auditing

Sustainable harvesting certification schemes and buyer codes audit permits, harvest plans, records, worker conditions and conservation actions. Keep documents organised: permits, maps, harvest plans, training records, harvest records, monitoring data, incident reports and alien clearing records. Close out audit findings promptly.

Community and stakeholders

Engage landowners, conservation authorities, fire protection associations and local communities. Wild harvesting often provides important rural employment; fair treatment and skills development strengthen the operation.

Safety

Plan for remote work: communication, emergency evacuation routes, heat and lightning protocols, snake and bee awareness, and safe vehicle transport of workers.

Key points

  • Hold valid permits and landowner permission for every site.
  • Base the harvest plan on a resource inventory, limits, rest and exclusion zones.
  • Train teams and pay in ways that reward compliance.
  • Monitor populations and adjust limits when they decline.
  • Keep complete records for certification and audits.

quiz.question: Why should reseeder species often have higher seed retention than resprouters?

options.text: Reseeders are killed by fire and rely on seed to recover

quiz.question: Which payment approach helps prevent over-harvesting?

options.text: Rewarding quality and compliance, not just volume

quiz.question: What should a manager do if monitoring shows a population is declining?

options.text: Reduce harvest limits or extend rest periods

quiz.question: Which areas are typically exclusion zones in a harvest plan?

options.text: Wetlands, riparian areas and threatened species populations

quiz.question: Why should the harvest plan be aligned with orders?

options.text: To avoid cutting stems that are wasted
